lesson.title: The Translator Molecule: tRNA's Cloverleaf Design
lesson.summary: Transfer RNA folds back on itself into a cloverleaf-shaped molecule with an anticodon at one end and an amino acid attachment site at the other, physically linking the genetic code to protein synthesis.
lesson.body:
A tRNA is a single strand of RNA, built from the same nucleotides as any other RNA molecule, but it does not stay stretched out in a simple line the way mRNA does. It folds back on itself, and stretches of it pair up with other stretches according to the same base pairing rules used in codon-anticodon recognition, creating a secondary structure that looks, when drawn out flat, like a four-leafed clover. That structure has a name for each arm: the acceptor stem, the D arm, the anticodon arm, and the T arm, along with a smaller variable region whose length differs somewhat from one tRNA to another.

Two of these regions matter more than the rest for what a tRNA actually does. In the middle of the cloverleaf, the anticodon arm ends in a loop that exposes the three-nucleotide anticodon described in the previous chapter, the sequence that pairs directly with an mRNA codon. At the opposite end of the molecule, the acceptor stem ends in a short, nearly universal sequence, CCA, at its 3' tip. This is where the tRNA's matching amino acid actually gets attached, through a covalent bond formed by an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase, the subject of the next chapter. So a single tRNA molecule has two functional ends doing two different jobs at once: one end reads the genetic code by pairing with mRNA, and the other end physically carries the amino acid that code calls for.

The flat cloverleaf is only a simplified way of drawing the molecule; in three dimensions, it folds further into a compact L-shape, with the anticodon at one tip of the L and the amino acid attachment site at the other, held apart from each other in space. tRNA molecules also contain a number of chemically modified nucleotides beyond the standard four, unusual bases that help stabilize this folded shape and, in some cases, contribute to the flexible wobble pairing at the third codon position. All of this folding serves one purpose: it lets the tRNA fit precisely into a ribosome while simultaneously presenting its anticodon to the mRNA and its amino acid cargo to the growing protein chain.
